scenario.title: Support backlog
scenario.initial_request: Build a chatbot so customers stop waiting for answers about refunds

M-IBAN-FAIL-RATE.name: Share of refund_failures records with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT
M-IBAN-FAIL-RATE.numerator: refund records with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT in payment-db.refund_failures
M-IBAN-FAIL-RATE.denominator: all sampled refund_failures records in payment-db

M-TICKET-RESPONSE-DURATION.name: Median time from ticket creation to first response

M-BACKLOG-SIZE.name: Count of open refund-linked tickets pending refund completion
M-BACKLOG-SIZE.population: ticket-db tickets linked to payment-db refunds not yet completed

F-01.statement: 5 of 5 sampled payment-db refund_failures records (R-0..R-4) have status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT.

F-02.statement: ticket-db.response_times across 900 tickets shows median_hours=2.0 against sla_hours=24.

CL-01.statement: Build a chatbot so customers stop waiting for answers about refunds

CL-02.statement: Customers wait forever; a chatbot would answer instantly.

H-RESPONSE-SPEED.statement: The backlog exists because customers wait too long to receive answers about refund status, so a chatbot that answers faster would resolve it.

H-PAYMENT-PROCESSING-DELAY.statement: The real bottleneck is slow refund processing in the payment system (DA-PAY), so tickets stay open/unanswered because there is no refund status yet to communicate, not because of answering speed.

H-INFO-VISIBILITY-GAP.statement: Support agents lack timely access to refund status data (DA-PAY) when resolving tickets (DA-TCK), causing delayed answers even though the underlying refund may already be processed.

H-TICKET-VOLUME-OVERLOAD.statement: The backlog is driven by ticket volume exceeding support capacity, independent of how fast any single answer is delivered.

H-IBAN-FORMAT-FAILURE.statement: Refunds fail outright in payment-db due to invalid IBAN format, so the backlog persists because these refunds never complete, independent of response speed, visibility, or ticket volume.

interpretation_history.interpretation: E-01 (payment-db.refund_failures, authoritative, complete) shows 5 of 5 sampled refund records are in status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT, i.e. these refunds never completed because of a data-validation rejection in the payment system, not because of answer latency.

ticket-db.response_times (900 tickets, authoritative/complete) shows a median response of 2.0 hours against a 24-hour SLA, meaning tickets are being answered well within the target speed rather than being delayed by slow responses.

E-03.content: Customers wait forever; a chatbot would answer instantly.

interpretation_history.interpretation: SH-SUP (same stakeholder behind CL-01, noted bias toward response-speed framing) restates the claim that slow answers cause the backlog and a chatbot would fix it. This is a non-authoritative reiteration of CL-01, adding no new evidence and not addressing the authoritative findings (E-01 IBAN failures, E-02 SLA compliance) that already contradict it.

U-FAILURE-MODE-DISTRIBUTION.question: Does the full population of backlogged refunds (beyond the 5-record sample) show the same IBAN-format-failure pattern, or do other failure modes also contribute?
U-FAILURE-MODE-DISTRIBUTION.decision_impact: Determines whether remediation should target IBAN validation only or also address other failure modes (e.g. the bank-api DEGRADED/ACCESS_DENIED condition noted in the recovery log).
U-FAILURE-MODE-DISTRIBUTION.resolution_path: Query payment-db for the complete refund_failures distribution across the full backlog, not just the 5-record sample.
U-FAILURE-MODE-DISTRIBUTION.safe_placeholder: Treat only confirmed FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT records as in-scope for remediation until the full distribution is analyzed.

U-CANDIDATE-HYPOTHESES-UNTESTE.question: Do H-PAYMENT-PROCESSING-DELAY (slow processing in DA-PAY) or H-INFO-VISIBILITY-GAP (agents lacking refund-status visibility) contribute additional backlog beyond IBAN failures?
U-CANDIDATE-HYPOTHESES-UNTESTE.decision_impact: If either holds, remediation must also address processing speed or agent visibility into DA-PAY, not just IBAN validation.
U-CANDIDATE-HYPOTHESES-UNTESTE.resolution_path: Test H-PAYMENT-PROCESSING-DELAY and H-INFO-VISIBILITY-GAP against payment-db processing timestamps and ticket-db agent-access patterns.
U-CANDIDATE-HYPOTHESES-UNTESTE.safe_placeholder: Treat IBAN-format failure as the primary confirmed cause; do not assume processing delay or visibility gaps without further evidence.

U-BANK-API-DEGRADATION-RELEVAN.question: Does the DEGRADED/ACCESS_DENIED state of bank-api (recovery_decision, seq 50) affect analysis or future correction of the IBAN-failed refunds?
U-BANK-API-DEGRADATION-RELEVAN.decision_impact: If investigation or correction of IBAN data depends on bank-api, that work may be blocked until access is restored.
U-BANK-API-DEGRADATION-RELEVAN.resolution_path: Check whether IBAN root-cause analysis or correction depends on bank-api, and track its health status before relying on it.
U-BANK-API-DEGRADATION-RELEVAN.safe_placeholder: Limit current analysis to payment-db and ticket-db (both HEALTHY); do not assume bank-api access is required or available.

A-SAMPLE-REPRESENTATIVE.statement: The 5 sampled refund_failures records (E-01) are representative of the broader refund backlog rather than an isolated subset.

A-BACKLOG-IS-REFUND-LINKED.statement: The backlog SH-SUP references consists of tickets tied to refunds that have not completed, consistent with E-02 showing responses are already fast rather than a separate ticket-volume problem.

SC-ROOT-CAUSE-CONFIRMED.statement: Full population of payment-db refund_failures is analyzed to confirm whether IBAN-format failures (not response speed) account for the backlog.
SC-ROOT-CAUSE-CONFIRMED.threshold: sample (n=5) expanded to full backlog population
SC-ROOT-CAUSE-CONFIRMED.validation_method: Run payment-db.refund_failures query across the entire backlog and compare the failure-status distribution to the 5-record sample.

SC-IBAN-FAILURE-REDUCED.statement: The rate of refunds failing due to FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT decreases after remediation.
SC-IBAN-FAILURE-REDUCED.validation_method: Re-run payment-db.refund_failures query after remediation and compare the failure rate to the baseline.

SC-BACKLOG-DECREASING.statement: The count of open refund-linked tickets caused by incomplete refunds decreases after remediation.
SC-BACKLOG-DECREASING.validation_method: Track the ticket-db backlog count tied to unresolved payment-db refunds before and after remediation.

VOB-U-FAILURE-MODE-DISTRIBUTION.unresolved_question: Does the full population of backlogged refunds (beyond the 5-record sample) show the same IBAN-format-failure pattern, or do other failure modes also contribute?
VOB-U-FAILURE-MODE-DISTRIBUTION.reason_deferred: deferred at DEFINE Gate; safe placeholder: Treat only confirmed FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT records as in-scope for remediation until the full distribution is analyzed.
VOB-U-FAILURE-MODE-DISTRIBUTION.validation_method: Query payment-db for the complete refund_failures distribution across the full backlog, not just the 5-record sample.

VOB-R-2.unresolved_question: Do H-PAYMENT-PROCESSING-DELAY or H-INFO-VISIBILITY-GAP contribute to the backlog beyond IBAN-format failures, which would change how correlate_tickets_with_failed_refunds output should be interpreted?
VOB-R-2.reason_deferred: proposed by reasoner R-11: Both candidate hypotheses are listed as affecting correlate_tickets_with_failed_refunds:DA-TCK and remain untested (status CANDIDATE), so shipping that action without testing them risks mis-attributing backlog composition.
VOB-R-2.validation_method: Analyze payment-db processing-time distribution for backlogged refunds and audit whether ticket-db agents had timely DA-PAY visibility when tickets were last updated, then compare results against both candidate hypotheses.
required_evidence: payment-db processing-time records for backlogged refunds
ticket-db agent access/update timestamps relative to refund status changes

VOB-R-3.unresolved_question: Does the bank-api DEGRADED/ACCESS_DENIED NOT_TRANSIENT HOLD (seq 50) permanently block correction of existing FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT refunds, or is there a resolvable cause or alternate correction path?
VOB-R-3.reason_deferred: proposed by reasoner R-11: SR-EXISTING-FAILURES-REMEDIATIO, the remedy that would actually correct backlogged refunds, is marked constraint_feasible=false specifically because of this unresolved bank-api HOLD.
VOB-R-3.validation_method: Escalate to the owning team to determine whether ACCESS_DENIED is a permanent policy restriction or a resolvable credential/config issue, then confirm via a bank-api health re-check.
required_evidence: Owner response on ACCESS_DENIED root cause
Confirmation of restored bank-api HEALTHY status or an approved alternate correction path

problem_definition.requested_solution: Build a chatbot so customers stop waiting for answers about refunds (CL-01, initial request from SH-SUP).
symptoms: Refund-related support tickets remain open/backlogged, which prompted the initial request for a chatbot to speed up answers (CL-01).
Ticket response times are actually fast (E-02: median 2.0h vs 24h SLA), yet the backlog persists, indicating response speed is not the driver.
problem_definition.root_problem: Refund-linked support tickets stay backlogged because the underlying refunds fail outright in payment-db due to invalid IBAN format (E-01: 5/5 sampled refund_failures = FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT), not because agents respond slowly (E-02: median response 2.0h vs 24h SLA); tickets stay open awaiting a refund completion that never occurs.

trace.summary: Refund-linked support tickets stay backlogged because the underlying refunds fail outright in payment-db due to invalid IBAN format (E-01: 5/5 sampled refund_failures = FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT), not because agents respond slowly (E-02: median response 2.0h vs 24h SLA); tickets stay open awaiting a refund completion that never occurs.

details.requested_solution: Build a chatbot so customers stop waiting for answers about refunds (CL-01, initial request from SH-SUP).

trace.summary: Deterministic queries can run, but judging whether H-PAYMENT-PROCESSING-DELAY or H-INFO-VISIBILITY-GAP contribute beyond IBAN failures, and what to do about the bank-api ACCESS_DENIED/NOT_TRANSIENT HOLD (seq 50), requires reasoning over ambiguous, untested evidence.

structural_remedies.description: Add real-time IBAN format validation at the point refunds are created/submitted so malformed IBANs are rejected or corrected before entering payment-db, preventing new FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT cases.
structural_remedies.rationale: This is an upstream intake/system change to the refund process; no constraint in state blocks ORG-1 from making it, but implementing and deploying it exceeds what can be verified within the remaining 225-minute budget during a DESIGN-phase analysis.; residual gap: Does not remediate the existing backlog of already-failed refunds (R-0..R-4 and the broader population), and leaves open whether other failure modes beyond IBAN format also contribute (U-FAILURE-MODE-DISTRIBUTION, VOB-U-FAILURE-MODE-DISTRIBUTION).

structural_remedies.description: Establish an ownership-assigned process (e.g. payments ops) to identify all FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT refunds in payment-db, obtain corrected IBANs from customers, resubmit the refunds, and close/update the linked DA-TCK tickets once completed.
structural_remedies.rationale: Identification via payment-db (HEALTHY) is feasible, but actual resubmission/correction likely routes through bank-api, which recent_events seq 50 shows is DEGRADED with an ACCESS_DENIED HOLD marked NOT_TRANSIENT and no fallback path, blocking the correction action itself.; residual gap: Backlogged refunds cannot actually be resolved until the bank-api access issue is addressed or an alternate correction path is found; U-BANK-API-DEGRADATION-RELEVANT remains OPEN.

structural_remedies.description: Expand the IBAN-failure analysis from the 5-record sample to the full population of backlogged payment-db refund_failures to confirm the failure-mode distribution before release, satisfying SC-ROOT-CAUSE-CONFIRMED.
structural_remedies.rationale: payment-db is HEALTHY and read-only querying is already within PD-1's intended_scope (analyze_refund_failure_distribution:DA-PAY), making this a deterministic, low-cost extension of existing analysis.; residual gap: Confirms or refines the diagnosis but does not itself fix any failures; VOB-U-FAILURE-MODE-DISTRIBUTION remains open until this run completes and is reviewed.

structural_remedies.description: Introduce an automated data linkage (config/integration) so DA-TCK tickets reflect current DA-PAY refund status, closing or updating tickets automatically once a refund is resolved, reducing agent reliance on manual lookups.
structural_remedies.rationale: No stated constraint prohibits a payment-ticket status integration, but building and validating such a cross-system linkage is an engineering effort beyond the remaining analysis budget.; residual gap: Only mitigates visibility/dwell-time symptoms (H-INFO-VISIBILITY-GAP, still CANDIDATE/untested per U-CANDIDATE-HYPOTHESES-UNTESTED); does not stop refunds from failing in the first place.

decision_log.rationale: causal chain: A customer requests a refund; a ticket is opened (DA-TCK) and the refund is submitted to the payment system (DA-PAY) for processing. → The payment system validates IBAN format before completing the refund. → IBAN format validation fails for the refund (status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT), so the refund never completes (E-01/F-01). → Because the refund never completes, the linked ticket cannot be resolved, regardless of how fast the agent replies (E-02/F-02 shows replies are already fast). → These uncompleted, IBAN-rejected refunds accumulate as the observed refund-ticket backlog.; rejected framings: [('H-RESPONSE-SPEED', "Contradicted by both E-01 (refunds fail outright on IBAN format, unrelated to speed) and E-02 (median response 2.0h is well within the 24h SLA); only supported by the stakeholder's own non-authoritative restatement (E-03), which adds no new evidence."), ('H-TICKET-VOLUME-OVERLOAD', 'Contradicted by E-02, which shows tickets are answered well within SLA despite volume, so capacity overload is not the mechanism.')]
[CONDITIONAL] critical unknown U-FAILURE-MODE-DISTRIBUTION deferred to VOB-U-FAILURE-MODE-DISTRIBUTION

framing_assertion.rationale: SH-SUP's initial request ('chatbot so customers stop waiting') asserts the backlog's root cause is slow response/communication speed, fixable by automating answers; SH-SUP has stated potential_bias 'frames everything as response speed'.

hypotheses.statement: The backlog exists because customers wait too long to receive answers about refund status, so a chatbot that answers faster would resolve it.
hypotheses.rationale: This is SH-SUP's own framing (support lead, flagged bias 'frames everything as response speed'); if false, building a chatbot would not address the real bottleneck.

hypotheses.statement: The real bottleneck is slow refund processing in the payment system (DA-PAY), so tickets stay open/unanswered because there is no refund status yet to communicate, not because of answering speed.
hypotheses.rationale: If refunds themselves are slow, a chatbot can only relay 'still pending' faster, not shorten the underlying wait, requiring a fix to process P-REF instead of a communication tool.
discriminating_evidence: correlation between ticket open duration and refund settlement timing

hypotheses.statement: Support agents lack timely access to refund status data (DA-PAY) when resolving tickets (DA-TCK), causing delayed answers even though the underlying refund may already be processed.
hypotheses.rationale: If the gap is a data/handoff visibility problem between ticket-db and payment-db rather than conversational speed, the fix would be system integration or agent tooling, not a customer-facing chatbot.
discriminating_evidence: cross-reference of DA-TCK ticket timestamps against DA-PAY payment status timestamps
tool_surface entries for ticket-db and payment-db as separate read-only sources

hypotheses.statement: The backlog is driven by ticket volume exceeding support capacity, independent of how fast any single answer is delivered.
hypotheses.rationale: If volume/staffing is the driver, automating responses may reduce symptom visibility but not the underlying capacity shortfall, pointing toward staffing or ticket-deflection solutions instead.
discriminating_evidence: ratio of ticket volume to response times in ticket-db

actions.question: What do actual ticket response-time and volume metrics in DA-TCK show for refund-related tickets?
actions.expected_information_gain: Reveals whether delay is in answering speed, ticket backlog volume, or waiting on upstream payment data, directly separating H-RESPONSE-SPEED from H-TICKET-VOLUME-OVERLOAD and H-INFO-VISIBILITY-GAP.
actions.decision_impact_rationale: Determines whether a speed-focused solution (chatbot) is even the right lever versus staffing/visibility fixes.
actions.why_now: CL-01 (stakeholder claim) asserts response_speed as cause but is UNVERIFIED; this is the authoritative read-only source (DA-TCK) that can confirm or refute it.

actions.question: How frequently and for how long do refunds in DA-PAY actually fail or stall before completion?
actions.expected_information_gain: Shows whether refunds are genuinely stuck/failing in processing (supports H-PAYMENT-PROCESSING-DELAY) or completing fine while agents lack visibility (supports H-INFO-VISIBILITY-GAP).
actions.decision_impact_rationale: If refunds are failing in payment-db this is a CRITICAL-impact root cause that a chatbot cannot fix, redirecting the whole intervention.
actions.why_now: H-PAYMENT-PROCESSING-DELAY has CRITICAL decision_impact and is still CANDIDATE; this is the most direct authoritative data source naming refund processing failures.

actions.question: Does bank-side settlement status show delays that would explain refunds not yet being processed?
actions.expected_information_gain: Would confirm or rule out bank settlement latency as the exact mechanism behind H-PAYMENT-PROCESSING-DELAY, distinct from internal refund-failure handling.
actions.decision_impact_rationale: If settlement itself is the bottleneck, no internal process or chatbot change addresses it, which is decision-critical.
actions.why_now: H-PAYMENT-PROCESSING-DELAY names processing/settlement as the mechanism, but bank-api is not listed in scenario.tool_surface (only ticket-db, payment-db are); flag this authority/scope mismatch before executing.

actions.question: Can SH-SUP describe, concretely, what information agents can see about a refund's status at the moment they answer a ticket?
actions.expected_information_gain: Could surface whether agents lack a view into DA-PAY (supporting H-INFO-VISIBILITY-GAP) but is lower-value since SH-SUP already shows a known bias toward framing everything as response speed.
actions.decision_impact_rationale: Useful context on current agent workflow but limited discriminative power given stated stakeholder bias; data-source queries are preferred first.
actions.why_now: CL-01 is an unverified stakeholder claim from this same person; a follow-up interview can probe mechanism detail that raw metrics alone won't reveal, but should run after/alongside the authoritative data queries.

proposal.root_problem: Refund-linked support tickets stay backlogged because the underlying refunds fail outright in payment-db due to invalid IBAN format (E-01: 5/5 sampled refund_failures = FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT), not because agents respond slowly (E-02: median response 2.0h vs 24h SLA); tickets stay open awaiting a refund completion that never occurs.
proposal.requested_solution: Build a chatbot so customers stop waiting for answers about refunds (CL-01, initial request from SH-SUP).
symptoms: Refund-related support tickets remain open/backlogged, which prompted the initial request for a chatbot to speed up answers (CL-01).
Ticket response times are actually fast (E-02: median 2.0h vs 24h SLA), yet the backlog persists, indicating response speed is not the driver.
causal_chain: A customer requests a refund; a ticket is opened (DA-TCK) and the refund is submitted to the payment system (DA-PAY) for processing.
The payment system validates IBAN format before completing the refund.
IBAN format validation fails for the refund (status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT), so the refund never completes (E-01/F-01).
Because the refund never completes, the linked ticket cannot be resolved, regardless of how fast the agent replies (E-02/F-02 shows replies are already fast).
These uncompleted, IBAN-rejected refunds accumulate as the observed refund-ticket backlog.

assumptions.statement: The 5 sampled refund_failures records (E-01) are representative of the broader refund backlog rather than an isolated subset.
The backlog SH-SUP references consists of tickets tied to refunds that have not completed, consistent with E-02 showing responses are already fast rather than a separate ticket-volume problem.

Evidence contradicts the response-speed framing: E-01 (payment-db.refund_failures, 5/5 sampled records) shows refunds are failing outright with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT; E-02 (ticket-db.response_times, 900 tickets) shows median response of 2.0h against a 24h SLA, i.e. agents are already fast.

Root problem as defined in PD-1: refund-linked tickets stay backlogged because refunds fail outright in payment-db due to invalid IBAN format, not because of slow agent responses; tickets wait for a refund completion that never occurs.
DEFINE gate result was CONDITIONAL_PASS (seq 81), deferring the critical unknown U-FAILURE-MODE-DISTRIBUTION to VOB-U-FAILURE-MODE-DISTRIBUTION rather than blocking the whole problem definition.

What was released: correlate_tickets_with_failed_refunds:DA-TCK and monitor_ticket_response_sla:DA-TCK, matching the solution_design release_scope; the DA-PAY-based analyze_refund_failure_distribution action was withheld because VOB-U-FAILURE-MODE-DISTRIBUTION is OPEN and required_before=BEFORE_RELEASE.

The analyze_refund_failure_distribution:DA-PAY action was explicitly withheld from this release because its blocking verification obligation (VOB-U-FAILURE-MODE-DISTRIBUTION) was required to be resolved before release and was not.
Remediation of root cause (e.g. real-time IBAN validation at refund submission, SR-IBAN-INTAKE-VALIDATION) was identified as a needed fix but left unfinished/not implemented in this release.

The release carries a CONDITIONAL_PASS from the DEFINE gate rather than a full pass, meaning some problem-definition items were deferred as tracked VOBs instead of being fully resolved before proceeding.
proposal.summary: The stakeholder SH-SUP initially asked for a chatbot to stop customers waiting for refund answers (CL-01), framing the backlog as a response-speed issue (also restated non-authoritatively as E-03). Investigation established a different root cause: payment-db evidence (E-01) shows all 5 sampled refund_failures records are status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT, meaning refunds are failing outright, while ticket-db evidence (E-02) shows median response time is 2.0h against a 24h SLA, i.e. agents already respond quickly. These two authoritative pieces of evidence contradict the response-speed hypothesis (H-RESPONSE-SPEED, REJECTED) and support H-IBAN-FORMAT-FAILURE (SUPPORTED), leading the problem definition PD-1 to state the real root cause is refunds never completing due to invalid IBAN format, not slow agent answers. The DEFINE gate returned CONDITIONAL_PASS, deferring one high-criticality unknown (failure-mode distribution across the full backlog, beyond the 5-record sample) as a verification obligation (VOB-U-FAILURE-MODE-DISTRIBUTION) rather than blocking everything. The release decision is RELEASE_WITH_KNOWN_LIMITATION: the scope that was actually released is the ticket/refund correlation and SLA-monitoring work (correlate_tickets_with_failed_refunds:DA-TCK, monitor_ticket_response_sla:DA-TCK), while the DA-PAY-based failure-distribution analysis was withheld because its blocking verification obligation remains open and was required before release. A second verification obligation touching the released scope (VOB-R-2, about untested contributing hypotheses) was judged non-critical, and a third (VOB-R-3, about the DEGRADED bank-api tool blocking correction of existing failed refunds) falls outside the released scope and is only required before any future protected action. The release is accompanied by multiple explicit known limitations, listed below, covering data completeness, untested hypotheses, the degraded tool, and unfinished remediation work.
